Week 2
The shape of probability.
## What did probability give us? {.concept-slide}
Recall from Week 1
Experiment
→
Possible outcomes
→
Events
→
Numbers
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$ A \subseteq \Omega \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbb{P}(A)\in[0,1] $$
::: ::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Probability gives numerical structure to uncertainty.
::: ::: {.notes} Use this slide to reconnect students to Week 1 without spending too much time reviewing formal probability spaces. ::: ## Outcomes do not all occur equally often {.motivation-slide}
Two pharmaceutical motivations
Tablet press
The nominal target is 2.000 g. But every tablet is not exactly 2.000 g.
Automatic camera inspection
A faulty tablet is expected in 0.1% of presses. How long can the line run without seeing a rejection?
$0.999^{1,000}$  vs.  $0.999^{1,000,000}$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A distribution describes how probability is spread across possible outcomes.
::: ::: {.notes} These examples foreshadow both continuous and discrete distributions. Tablet mass is continuous. Fault/no fault per press is binary, and the waiting time until first failure is discrete. Do not calculate yet. Use these as curiosity hooks. ::: ## A distribution is the shape of uncertainty {.concept-slide}
From isolated events to a whole pattern
One event
A single probability question:
$\mathbb{P}(A)=0.30$
Many possible outcomes
Probability is allocated across the entire outcome space.
1
2
3
4
5
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The same probability rules still apply — but now we study the whole shape.
::: ::: {.notes} This slide introduces the word “shape” intentionally. Students should begin to imagine a distribution as the pattern of probability weights over possible values. ::: ## Two fundamentally different worlds {.concept-slide}
Discrete versus continuous
Discrete random variable
Possible values are separated. Individual values can have positive probability.
Fair die: $X\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$
Continuous random variable
Possible values fill an interval. Probability belongs to ranges, not exact points.
Random number: $X\in[0,1]$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Discrete probability lives on values. Continuous probability lives over intervals.
::: ::: {.notes} Use a fair die rather than a coin as the flagship discrete-uniform example. Reserve the coin for Bernoulli. The main conceptual target: for continuous variables, asking for exactly one value is not the same kind of question as for discrete variables. ::: ## Probability mass versus probability density {.math-slide}
The height means different things
Probability mass function (PMF)
The bar height is the exact probability of that point.
$p(x) = \mathbb{P}(X=x)$
1
2
3
1/6 4
5
6
$\mathbb{P}(X=4) = 1/6 \approx 0.167$
Probability density function (PDF)
Curve height is density. Area under the curve is probability.
$\mathbb{P}(a < X < b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$
Area = 0.20
0 0.4 0.6 1
$\mathbb{P}(X=0.5) = 0 \quad \text{vs.} \\ \mathbb{P}(0.4 < X < 0.6) = 0.20$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For continuous variables, probability requires width — an interval, not a single point.
::: ::: {.notes} This is one of the most important conceptual slides of Week 2. Let students sit with the paradox: a possible exact value has probability zero under a continuous distribution. Use the phrase: “A point has no width, so it has no area.” ::: ## Where can the variable live? {.concept-slide}
Support
Fair die
Only six possible values.
123456
Uniform number
Any real value between 0 and 1.
0$[0,1]$1
Waiting time
Cannot be negative, but can be arbitrarily long.
0$[0,\infty)$∞
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The support of a distribution is the set of values the random variable can take.
::: ::: {.notes} Support is useful vocabulary. Tie it to biological and pharmaceutical constraints: concentrations cannot be negative; proportions are between 0 and 1; counts are nonnegative integers. ::: ## Everything must add up to one {.math-slide}
The same conservation rule in two forms
$$ \sum_x p(x)=1 $$
$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx=1 $$
discrete pieces add
continuous area integrates
::: {.notes} This slide reinforces a single intuitive conservation law: all probability goes somewhere. In discrete cases, add the pieces; in continuous cases, integrate the area. ::: ## One definition unifies both worlds {.math-slide}
Cumulative distribution function
$$ F(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x) $$
discrete CDF jumps
continuous CDF flows
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The CDF always answers the same question: how much probability has accumulated up to this point?
::: ::: {.notes} Stress that the CDF is often easier to use for “at most” or “less than” questions. It will become crucial for p-values, quantiles and confidence intervals later. ::: ## Watch probability accumulate {.exercise-slide}
Interactive concept slide
Move the cutoff. Probability to the left becomes the CDF value.
Distribution
Standard Normal
CDF value F(x)
0.500
::: {.notes} This widget is intentionally simple: a standard normal curve, a vertical cutoff, and the shaded probability to the left. It visually links the PDF to the CDF. ::: ## What probability are you asking for? {.concept-slide}
The wording determines the area
Exactly
$\mathbb{P}(X=x)$
meaningful for discrete values
At most
$\mathbb{P}(X\leq x)$
lower cumulative probability
At least
$\mathbb{P}(X\geq x)$
upper tail probability
Between
$\mathbb{P}(a
interval probability
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
“Exactly”, “at most”, “at least” and “between” are different probability questions.
::: ::: {.notes} This slide prepares the tablet mass widget. Emphasize how often students answer the wrong probability question because the wording is imprecise. ::: ## Tablet press laboratory {.exercise-slide}
Interactive slide for students at home
model $X\sim \mathcal{N}(2.000,0.008^2)$
region 1.990–2.010 g
probability 0.789
::: {.notes} Use this as the central interactive slide for Week 2. The key message is not numerical precision; it is that the probability question determines which area under the curve is relevant. Suggested live sequence: ask for between 1.99 and 2.01, then switch to at least 1.99. Same bound, completely different probability question. ::: ## Meet the normal distribution {.math-slide}
After the intuition, the notation
Notation
$X\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$
Two parameters uniquely define the model: location and spread.
Density
$$f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}$$
Recognize the formula. Do not memorize it.
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For the Gaussian model, $\mu$ moves the center and $\sigma$ controls the spread.
Why Gaussian normal distribution is so common in nature: it models an outcome that is the sum of many tiny independent contributions.
::: ::: {.notes} Tell students that formula recognition is enough here. They should understand what the parameters do and how to interpret probability regions. ::: ## What do μ and σ actually do? {.exercise-slide}
Interactive parameter intuition
Current model
𝒩(0, 1²)
::: {.notes} Demonstrate μ first while keeping σ fixed: the curve slides. Then demonstrate σ while keeping μ fixed: the curve spreads and flattens. ::: ## The empirical rule {.concept-slide}
A useful landmark for Gaussian variation
68.3% inside $\mu\pm1\sigma$
95.4% inside $\mu\pm2\sigma$
99.7% inside $\mu\pm3\sigma$
::: {.notes} Say “roughly 68–95–99.7” when speaking. These percentages apply specifically to the normal distribution, not every bell-shaped curve. ::: ## Moments and distribution characteristics {.section-break}
Part II
The parameters of probability distributions
We now see what numbers characterize the distributions.
## Quantiles cut probability, not distance {.concept-slide}
Percentiles and inverse CDF thinking
5th percentile 5% of probability lies below it.
Median 50% below and 50% above.
95th percentile 95% lies below it.
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A quantile is a value chosen by accumulated probability.
::: ::: {.notes} This prepares later confidence intervals, reference ranges, p-values and percentile-based clinical interpretation. ::: ## Mean: where is the distribution centered? {.concept-slide}
Expected value as a balance point
$$ E[X] = \sum_x x\,p(x) \quad\text{or}\quad E[X]=\int x f(x)\,dx $$
$E[X]$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The expected value (mean, also called **first moment**) is the balancing point of the probability distribution.
::: ::: {.notes} Use this as a physical metaphor, then remind students that the mean can be pulled by long tails. That sets up skewness. ::: ## Variance: how far do values wander? {.math-slide}
Second central moment
$$ \operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2], \qquad SD(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)} $$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Variance (also called **second central moment**) measures spread around the mean using squared deviations.
::: ::: {.notes} Students should know variance is in squared units and standard deviation returns to original units. Use tablet mass: variance in g² is less intuitive than SD in g. ::: ## Symmetry and skewness {.concept-slide}
Mean, median and mode can separate
Mean
Median
Mode
Left-skewed
Symmetric
Right-skewed
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For right-skewed shapes, the mean is often pulled toward the long right tail.
Skewness can be characterized with the **third central moment**.
::: ::: {.notes} State the mean/median/mode order as a visual heuristic, not a theorem for every possible distribution. Use examples: concentrations, residence times, income and many biological measurements can be right-skewed. ::: ## Why tails matter {.concept-slide}
Kurtosis as extreme-event propensity
Same center, very different probability of distant values.
Kurtosis is best remembered here as tail/extreme-value behavior.
Outliers may be surprising under one model and ordinary under another.
::: {.notes} Avoid the common oversimplification “kurtosis equals peakedness.” For this course, emphasize heavy tails and extreme values. ::: ## The Cauchy surprise {.concept-slide}
Not every distribution behaves politely
$E[X]$ is not defined
$\operatorname{Var}(X)$ is not defined
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The Gaussian is friendly. The Cauchy reminds us that not all distributions have familiar summaries.
::: ::: {.notes} This slide uses a CSS/SVG animation as the default. It is also an excellent candidate for a future Manim animation because the continuous motion carries mathematical meaning. The rigorous idea: if an angle is uniform and the intersection coordinate is tan(theta), the resulting distribution is Cauchy-like. ::: ## A map of named distributions {.concept-slide}
Learn mechanisms before formulas
Discrete mechanisms
Degenerateno uncertainty
Uniformfinite equal chances
Bernoullione yes/no trial
Binomialsuccesses in n trials
Geometrictrials until first success
Hypergeometricwithout replacement
Poissonevents in an interval
Continuous mechanisms
Diracpoint mass idealization
Uniformbounded equal density
Exponentialwaiting for one event
Gammawaiting for several events
Gaussianadditive variation
Log-normalmultiplicative positive variation
Paretoscaling/heavy tail
Cauchyvery heavy symmetric tails
::: {.notes} This replaces an encyclopedia of formulas with a map. Students should first learn which real-world mechanism each distribution represents. ::: ## Discrete: one trial to many trials {.math-slide}
Binary and finite equal-chance mechanisms
Degenerate
The outcome is fixed.
$\mathbb{P}(X=c)=1$
Discrete uniform
Finite outcomes equally likely.
$\mathbb{P}(X=x)=1/k$
Bernoulli
One yes/no experiment.
$\mathbb{P}(X=1)=p$
Binomial
Successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials.
$\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k}$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Coin toss: Bernoulli. Fair die: discrete uniform. Repeated responses: binomial.
::: ::: {.notes} Do not spend time deriving each formula. The story/mechanism is the learning target. The binomial formula will be used in exercises. ::: ## Discrete: counting and sampling {.math-slide}
Different sampling mechanisms create different distributions
Geometric
Trials until the first success.
$\mathbb{P}(T=t)=(1-p)^{t-1}p$
Hypergeometric
Sampling from a finite batch without replacement.
$\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\frac{\binom Kk\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom Nn}$
Poisson
Count events in a fixed exposure interval.
$\mathbb{P}(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Before calculating, identify the experiment that generated the count.
::: ::: {.notes} Use the tablet press example for geometric, batch sampling for hypergeometric, and dispensing errors or adverse events per exposure interval for Poisson. ::: ## Continuous: waiting and positive quantities {.math-slide}
Support and mechanism matter
Dirac delta
Point mass in continuous mathematics; not an ordinary PDF.
area = 1
Continuous uniform
Equal density on a bounded interval.
$f(x)=1/(b-a)$
Exponential
Waiting time until first event under constant rate.
$f(t)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t}$
Gamma
Waiting time until several events; flexible positive skew.
$X>0$
::: {.notes} Keep the Dirac delta simple: a mathematical idealization of all mass at one point. Do not teach generalized functions. ::: ## Continuous: shapes seen in real data {.math-slide}
Additive, multiplicative and heavy-tail behavior
Gaussian
Additive variation around a center.
$\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$
Log-normal
Positive values with multiplicative variability.
$\log X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\log},\sigma_{\log}^2)$
Pareto
Scaling behavior; few very large values.
heavy right tail
Cauchy
Very heavy symmetric tails; mean/variance undefined.
$\operatorname{Cauchy}(x_0,\gamma)$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Real scientific data often choose the distribution for us: counts, proportions, positive times, concentrations, extremes.
::: ::: {.notes} Pharmaceutical examples: concentration and clearance often right-skew; assay errors may be approximately Gaussian after calibration; adverse event counts may use Poisson-like models; extreme values require caution. ::: ## Which distribution describes the experiment? {.checkpoint-slide}
Checkpoint before calculation
A. 20 patients each respond or do not respond.
B. Count dispensing errors during an 8-hour shift.
C. Inspect 5 tablets from a finite batch containing 3 known defects.
D. Count presses until the first camera rejection.
E. Measure time until the first degradation event.
A → Binomial
B → Poisson
C → Hypergeometric
D → Geometric
E → Exponential
::: {.notes} Let students answer before revealing the right side. The major skill is matching question to distribution, not formula recall. ::: ## Probability laboratory {.exercise-slide}
Guided exercises
Geometric tablet-camera example
Fault probability per press is $p=0.001$. Probability of $1000$ error-free presses?
$0.999^{1000}\approx0.368$
Binomial patient group
$X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(20,0.30)$. What is the probability of (i) exactly, (ii) at most and (iii) at least 5 responses?
point vs cumulative probability
Hypergeometric batch sample
A batch has 20 tablets, 3 defective. Sample 5 without replacement.
finite population + no replacement
Normal tablet mass
$X\sim \mathcal{N}(2.000,0.008^2)$. Probability between 1.99 and 2.01 g?
area under density
::: {.notes} This slide is meant as a menu of short calculations. Work one or two live depending on time. The others can be take-home practice. ::: ## Point and cumulative binomial probabilities {.exercise-slide}
Interactive calculation intuition
Model
Binomial(20, 0.30)
Probability
—
::: {.notes} Use exactly, then at most, then at least for the same k. The bars should make the probability question visually unambiguous. ::: ## The catch {.concept-slide}
Week 2 synthesis
A distribution describes how probability is allocated.
Its shape determines which observations are plausible.
Different scientific mechanisms generate different distribution families.
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
But in real science, the true distribution and its parameters are almost never known.
::: ::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Next week: how can incomplete observations teach us about the process that generated them?
::: ::: {.notes} End with the transition from probability to statistics. Probability assumes a model and asks what observations are likely. Statistics observes data and asks what model or parameter values are plausible. :::

::: ::: {.notes} Use the tablet press example for geometric, batch sampling for hypergeometric, and dispensing errors or adverse events per exposure interval for Poisson. ::: ## Continuous: waiting and positive quantities {.math-slide}
Support and mechanism matter

area = 1

::: {.notes} Keep the Dirac delta simple: a mathematical idealization of all mass at one point. Do not teach generalized functions. ::: ## Continuous: shapes seen in real data {.math-slide}
Additive, multiplicative and heavy-tail behavior
Gaussian
Additive variation around a center.
$\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$
Log-normal
Positive values with multiplicative variability.
$\log X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\log},\sigma_{\log}^2)$
Pareto
Scaling behavior; few very large values.
heavy right tail
Cauchy
Very heavy symmetric tails; mean/variance undefined.
$\operatorname{Cauchy}(x_0,\gamma)$
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Real scientific data often choose the distribution for us: counts, proportions, positive times, concentrations, extremes.
::: ::: {.notes} Pharmaceutical examples: concentration and clearance often right-skew; assay errors may be approximately Gaussian after calibration; adverse event counts may use Poisson-like models; extreme values require caution. ::: ## Which distribution describes the experiment? {.checkpoint-slide}
Checkpoint before calculation
A. 20 patients each respond or do not respond.
B. Count dispensing errors during an 8-hour shift.
C. Inspect 5 tablets from a finite batch containing 3 known defects.
D. Count presses until the first camera rejection.
E. Measure time until the first degradation event.
A → Binomial
B → Poisson
C → Hypergeometric
D → Geometric
E → Exponential

Week 2 synthesis
A distribution describes how probability is allocated.
Its shape determines which observations are plausible.
Different scientific mechanisms generate different distribution families.
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
But in real science, the true distribution and its parameters are almost never known.
::: ::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Next week: how can incomplete observations teach us about the process that generated them?
::: ::: {.notes} End with the transition from probability to statistics. Probability assumes a model and asks what observations are likely. Statistics observes data and asks what model or parameter values are plausible. :::
